lawyer:
Md Humayun Kabir, Advocate and Israt Jahan, AAG -----For the Petitioner. 
Kashfia Hussain, AAG -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Ali, Hamza Mhalader (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the stoppage of the Government portion of the Monthly Salary due to the Petitioner from November, 1997 excluding the payment in the name of the Petitioner from the Monthly Pay Order (MPO) of November, 1997 should not be declared to have been made and passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the Respondents shall not be directed to pay the Government Portion of Salary to the Petitioner from November, 1997 as shown is the Monthly Pay Order (MPO) of November, 1997 against the name of the Petitioner therein and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The Petitioner comes before us as a retired teacher of a Madrasah who was first appointed to the Shah Ali Siddiquia Dakhil Madrasah on 15-12-1984 and joined in that position on 1-1-1985. It is noted that the first MPO enlistment of the Petitioner dates back to 1-6-1987 which he continued to receive up until November, 1997 when the Respondent No.4, Assistant Director (Special) Education, on behalf of the Respondent No.2, Director General, Secondary and Higher Secondary Education sent a letter to the Superintendent of the said Madrasah vide letter No. 14260/4 Bishesh dated 2-12-1997 seeking information relating to the appointment of five Junior Teachers as per seniority and inquired into the matter of two Additional Junior Teachers and required the said Madrasah to suspend payments of salary and benefits to all Junior Teachers until further orders but without assigning any further reason.

3. A Supplementary Affidavit filed on behalf of the Petitioner shows that the Petitioner continued to be deprived of his MPO entitlement for a continuous period up until 19-7-2006 when an MPO- restoration Order was issued from the office of the Respondent No.2, Director General directing the release of the Government Portion of the Petitioner's salary with retrospective effect from June, 2005. Given these circumstances the Petitioner's claim now extends to his MPO entitlement payable in arrears from November, 1997 to May 2005. This interim period between stoppage and restoration of the Petitioner's MPO entitlement spanning almost eight years witnessed the fact that of the teachers, who were initially adversely affected by the stop-page order of 2-12-1997 at least three individuals become the beneficiaries of restoration orders variously as early as in 1998 and 1999. It is also evident that efforts were duly made both by the Managing Committee of the Madrasah making representations before the concerned authority for releasing the amount claimed by the Petitioner with the Managing Committee duly acting further to a resolution adopted to that effect supplemented by individual efforts on the part of the Petitioner himself to establish contacts with the Respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 seeking a release of his MPO but all to no avail. It is noted further that the efforts on the part of the Petitioner, in particular, were aimed at fundamentally and significantly extracting from the concerned Respondents reasons for the initial stoppage of his MPO entitlement in 1997 that operated to his prejudice given that he had no opportunity given to him at the time to explain his position at the very initial stages as may have deterred such action to be taken against him. That appears to be the core issue submitted upon both in the Application and before this Court by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Humayun Kabir arguing that the decision for stop- page of MPO in 1997, taken evidently without any reason and without any prior notice, is indeed illegal, unlawful and tantamount to a colour able exercise of power. That illegality is all the more stark and blatant, submits the petitioner, given that his MPO entitlement amounts to a right of which he cannot be deprived without cogent grounds and reasons shown. Given further that the petitioner continued in service discharging his responsibility and obligations during much of the period when his MPO entitlement was stopped or remained suspended and up until its restoration as above with effect from 2005, that circumstance, it is argued, further fortifies his position as an individual who has very well acquired a vested right to the entitlement now claimed unless due, proper and substantive reasons can be shown by the Respondents to deprive him of the same. Mr Humayun Kabir has in this regard likened the deprivation suffered by the petitioner in these circumstances to a de facto penalty imposed by way of a punishment of the petitioner for reasons wholly unknown to him on all material dates, and for charges that he was never put on notice of There is further no evidence before this Court that any proceedings where ever drwan against him.

4. Indeed, the two crucial Orders in this case being the stoppage Order of 2-12-1997 (Annexure. 'D') and the restoration Order of 19-7-2006 (Annexure-'M') separated by over eight years, do not, upon a perusal, bring this Court any closer at detecting the true rationale behind or the objective grounds based on law, if any, that may have guided the Respondents in issuing either of the Orders. That state of affairs, it is found, has not been helped by the fact that no affidavit-in-Opposition has been filed in this Case and no specific instructions have been received by the Office of the Attorney-General in representing the Respondents' case in these proceedings. In particular, moreover, a "DIA Report" as appears to have formed the basis for the issuance of the Order of stoppage on 2-12-1997, and as is specifically referred to therein, could not be traced or retrieved from the Respondents notwithstanding the good efforts of the learned Assistant Attorneys- General Ms. Kashefa Hussain and Ms Israt Jahan acting on the instructions of this Court. Without going into the realm of speculation as to what may have motivated the issuance of the Orders above of both 1997 and 2006 this Court has now to dispose of this Rule on the bare facts that are found on record and on the basis of the common law tests that may rightfully be invoked and availed of by the petitioner in these circumstances.

5. Given that the right to office that one holds and the right to salary and entitlement one draws consequentially are vested in the office-bearer doing the continuance of his/her period of employment, the fundamental principle is that any action impairing enjoyment of such a vested right must be shown to have been objectively undertaken in accordance with law, ensuring, (hereby, both procedural and substantive safeguards. It follows, therefore, such impaimient, if found to be caused by action not in accordance with law, then any act resulting in such impairment or deprivation must be struck down as being illegal and without lawful authority (Md Amirul Islam vs Thana Nirbahi Officer, Lalpur, Natore reported in 2000 BLD 369 = 52 DLR 388; Md Shaw kat Ali vs Director General reported in 18 BLT 2010, 303). That principle is found by this Court to be attracted to the present facts and circumstances where it is not readily discernible as to how the Respondents justifiably issued either of the two orders of 1997 and 2006, the last order being but a partial and a limited attempt at restoration of the petitioner's MPO entitlement. It is this Court's finding in these circumstances that the principle enunciated above is by extension also applicable to the present facts and circumstances as the Respondents were not guided by law at all in dealing with the petitioner's case. This situation became all the more aggravated given that by the very nature of the right vested in the petitioner of holding an office and earning a salary, it was always incumbent upon the Respondents to curtail that right, if at all, by providing an opportunity to the petitioner individually to be heard, upon prior notice issued. That aspect of this case has been stressed upon by Mr Kabir repeatedly in the course of his submissions before this Court. That procedural safeguard not being adhered to the petitioner was equally at a loss, therefore, at clearly comprehending his predicament from a legal standpoint given that there were no indications forthcoming either with regard to the stoppage of his entitlement in 1997 or in the restoration order of 2006 of the legal standards and guidelines under which the Respondents sought to invoke their authority in this regard. In these circumstances and for want of a better explanation, it is indeed to be deduced that the withholding of the legal entitlement of the petitioner between November, 1997 and May 2005 tantamount to an imposition of a penalty illegally without any sanction of law (Secretary, Ministry of Education vs Anwar Hossain reported in 2 MLR (AD) 25 = 49 DLR (AD) 87). That being the case it necessarily follows, and Mr Kabir has satisfactorily argued to that effect, that the continued service provided by the petitioner during the eight year-period vests in him a right to salary and entitlement accrued which cannot be treated as bounty of the State in this case but instead as a debt owed to the petitioner in the form of salary and benefits payable in arrears (Quari Md Abdul Haleem vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 3 MLR (1998) 105 = 50 DLR 472).

6. Even if this Court were to make a supposition as to what the Respondents' rationale may have been to both stop or suspend-the petitioner's entitlement initially and to restore it, albeit partially, many years down the line, one may indeed look into the provisions বেসরকারী মাদ্রাসা শিক্ষক কর্মচারীর বেতনের সরকারি অংশ ও জনবল কাঠামো-১৯৯৫. Here to, Clause 11 (2) in particular appears to substantiate the petitioner's claim to entitlements rather than justify the action taken by the Respondents. Clause 11(2) reads thus:

“নতুন জনবল কাঠামো অনুযায়ী শিক্ষক ও কর্মচারীদের প্রাপ্যতা নির্ধারণের পর বেতন-ভাতাদির সরকারি অংশ প্রাপ্ত শিক্ষক ও কমৃচারীর সংখ্যা যদি প্রাপ্যতার অতিরিক্ত পদ সমূহ উদ্ধৃত্ত পদ বলে পরিগণিত হবে। এ ধরণের উদ্ধৃত্ত পদে নিয়োজিত শিক্ষক/কর্মচারীর পদ শূন্য হলে নতুন ভাবে পদে আর লোক নিয়োগ করা যাবেনা।”

7. Given that the petitioner stepped into the regime of the 1995 জনবল কাঠামো as an incumbent teacher who already had his MPO entitlement recognized since 1987, it would not stand to reason under Clause 11(2) to deprive him of such entitlement Oil the ground that beyond 1995 he, in any way, fell outside of the staffing-pattern sanctioned therein, thereby, disentitling him of his long-enjoyed MPO entitlement. Rather, on a true construction Clause 11(2) states that an incumbent teacher who is found upon the coming into effect of the 1995 জনবল কাঠামো to be MPO enlisted, but nevertheless appears to fall beyond the staffing pattern sanctioned in the 1995 জনবল কাঠামো shall nevertheless continue to receive the Government portion of his salary as before until he leaves his office by retirement or resignation or his said post falls vacant otherwise and after which such post considered to be উদ্বৃত পদে surplus post shall not be filled in by any fresh appointment. It is noted that the rationale is also evident in a similar provision being Clause 9(kha) of the বেসরকারী শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান (স্কুল, কলেজ, মাদ্রাসা ও কারিগরি শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান সমূহ) এর শিক্ষক ও কর্মচারীদের বেতন-ভাতাদির সরকারি অংশ প্রদান এবং জনবল কাঠামো সম্পর্কিত নির্দেশিকা, ২০১০. Even assuming that the Respondents were invoking the aforesaid provision of the 1995 জনবল কাঠামো then it was incumbent upon them to ask themselves the right question under the law or the operating guidelines and direct themselves, accordingly, to the provisions of Clause 11(2) and rationally and reasonably arrive at a finding beneficial to the petitioner that would, therefore, inevitably deter the issuance of the Order of suspension on 2-12-1997. Even from this point of view, there is found no objective and legal ground for the issuance of that Order in the manner that it was done.

<u>8. Given the above facts, findings and observations of this Court, and finding no overriding argument to the contrary to substantiate the position adopted by the Respondents in issuing the Order as above, this Court finds that the very disentitlement of the petitioner to his MPO as of November 1997 and the continuance of such disentitlement up until May 2005 has indeed been arbitrary and irregular. Such arbitrariness is made all the more blatant given by the evident violation of the petitioner's right to receive adequate and meaningful information at all material dates on decisions that were made to operate against him and to his prejudice for an unduly long period of time, thereby depriving him effectively of the opportunity to earn a livelihood and live in dignity as is an essential component of the right to life.</u>

9. Given these circumstances, the discontinuance of the petitioner's MPO is found to have been illegal and void ab initio given that the Respondents have miserably failed to show any authority in law that equipped them on any material date to act to the petitioner's prejudice. Here, this Court deems it fit to rely on the notion of restitution in integrum; thereby, enabling the petitioner as an injured party to be placed in the situation which ought to have prevailed had no injury been sustained by him by the issuance of the Order of 2-12-1997.

10. Accordingly, the Court hereby directs the concerned Respondents to ensure a payment to the petitioner of his claimed arrears as per the petitioner's MPO entitlement computed from November 1997 to May 2005 in accordance with law and within a period of 4(four) weeks from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order.

11. In light of the above, this Court finds merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued.

12. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with, in particular, the Order of 2-12-1997 being set aside on the grounds and reasons as above cited.

There is no Order as to costs.

End.
